content: The project manager is tasked with regularly reviewing monitoring data, including timestamps or details from paper-based forms that record the last menstrual period (LMP). This ensures proper implementation of the program. The manager must have previously identified key user indicators of high-fidelity implementation, such as the delivery of early newborn care, and should assess the time lag between the date of birth and the first visit to the mother and newborn. Users whose visits fall outside an acceptable time window should be interviewed to understand the causes of the delay and identify potential solutions. Fidelity monitoring must occur throughout the program's implementation. As the program progresses, the effort required for fidelity monitoring may decrease as technical, user, and external issues are identified and resolved. Continuous technical monitoring allows for immediate action if the digital health system fails to support the intervention as intended. Prompt responses to technical disruptions minimize downtime for users. Monitoring reports at the user level can reveal systematic errors, weaknesses in implementation, inappropriate technology use, poor worker motivation, or misunderstandings of the intervention content or best practices. User-based fidelity monitoring enables project managers to target specific users for retraining or counseling. Monitoring user fidelity is critical at all stages of maturity. However, as the number of users increases, it becomes essential to establish standardized monitoring procedures and reporting mechanisms. In early-stage pilot tests with a small number of users, field supervisors can gain insights into user strengths, weaknesses, and usage through field visits and cursory data reviews. In programs with a large number of users, such as 600, it becomes impractical for a small supervisory team to compile and act on monitoring findings. Displaying statistical performance data for many workers in tabular format is challenging, necessitating the use of graphical software or visual geographic systems via dashboard interfaces. As the intervention matures, monitoring must become increasingly automated and reported for decision-making. When monitoring the quality of digital health interventions, two aspects must be addressed: user capabilities and intervention content. Training large numbers of workers on digital health systems presents challenges, including low technical literacy, lack of prior exposure to technology, and resistance to changing long-standing work processes. Even within the same workforce, there may be significant variation in workers' comfort with hardware and software, often influenced by age and prior off-the-job experience with technology. For example, younger workers may be more tech-literate than their senior counterparts. It is essential to assess whether health workers are accurately entering information into the digital health system and whether gaps in user understanding hinder correct system use or intervention delivery. The quality of the intervention content is equally important. The content delivered by the digital health system, such as SMS messages, decision-support algorithms, or data collection forms, must be of the highest quality, informed by existing literature and formative research in the local context. This ensures the effectiveness of the intervention. Project managers must determine the key functionalities for system users and identify indicators to assess user readiness. These indicators may include phone operation skills, knowledge of system functionalities, data collection accuracy, or basic troubleshooting skills. Once the system is launched, quality monitoring should focus on data accuracy and regularity by identifying outliers or non-compliant users. Before launch, it is crucial to confirm that the intervention content aligns with international standards and is appropriate for the target community. Trainers are often best positioned to assess core competencies using checklists, but senior staff or trainers from different groups should also be involved to avoid bias. Project managers are responsible for the overall content of the intervention, but senior-level team members, such as principal investigators or project area officers, may contribute to content development and are ultimately accountable for its quality. Monitoring user comfort with the system is essential to determine readiness before launch. Regular assessments should continue throughout the intervention to ensure users operate the system as intended. Monitoring content quality typically occurs in the early stages of an intervention, with improvements made based on user feedback. Additional quality monitoring should ensure that updated content meets the intervention's original aims and maintains high quality. The findings from monitoring user quality allow trainers and supervisors to identify workers needing additional training, target specific areas for retraining, and bring all users to a baseline level of quality before launch. After launch, monitoring ensures a high level of quality is maintained. Real-time data from digital health systems enables faster feedback loops than traditional systems, allowing for near real-time course corrections in intervention delivery. If content quality is poor or unlikely to achieve the desired effect, adjustments must be made to improve this critical aspect of the intervention. If poor-quality content is identified after implementation has begun, project managers must prioritize content adjustments and continuous monitoring until the content is deemed sufficient to drive an effective intervention. Monitoring user quality becomes increasingly challenging and resource-intensive as the number of users and geographic coverage expand. Quality control checks on user ability to operate the digital health system are essential. For example, the KEMRI TextIT project used a trainee competency checklist to assess key smartphone and application functionalities. Another method for monitoring data accuracy involves issuing standard scenarios to trainees to reinforce training concepts, either through role-play or narrative exercises. Continued monitoring after launch should identify outliers or underperformers based on key indicators, such as the ability to correctly enter gestational age for pregnant women. Before implementation, project managers must ensure the digital health system functions properly. For example, SMS messages and scheduling must operate satisfactorily, and the health worker interface must perform as expected. Functionality monitoring before launch may involve creating and utilizing quality assurance (QA) test cases to outline expected outcomes for specific actions and record actual outcomes. Issues to check include whether SMS content is correct and whether messages are sent to the right phone numbers at the right time. Managers must verify that the system will deliver reminders to the correct families about their child’s upcoming vaccinations before they are due. Once the system's basic functionality is deemed acceptable, the project manager must verify its stability. Stability issues, such as frequent application crashes, may not always be identified during the pre-launch period. To assess stability, project managers and developers might review server downtime statistics, SMS failure rates, and the system's capacity to handle exceptionally high data burdens.
